```{r setup, include=FALSE}
# Preparation of the environment
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
library(tidyverse)
library(readr)
library(tseries)
library(forecast)

Introduction

This report focuses on the empirical analysis of five macroeconomic and utility time series from a developed country (primarily the US and France). The objective is to evaluate their stationarity, identify the most suitable autoregressive AR(p) models using OLS estimation, and provide short-term forecasts.
Problem I: Univariate Analysis and Forecasting
1. Descriptive Analysis and Time Series Properties

For the following variables, we analyze the level (often log-transformed) and the first difference to check for stationarity.
A. Consumer Price Index (CPI)

We utilize the log of the index to stabilize the variance over the long run.

'''
# Data Loading and cleaning
df1 <- read_csv("CPIAUCSL.csv", col_types = cols(observation_date = col_date(format = "%Y-%m-%d"), 
                                                 CPIAUCSL = col_number()))
df1$CPIAUCSL <- na.interp(df1$CPIAUCSL)
serie_prix <- ts(df1$CPIAUCSL, start = c(1947, 1), frequency = 12)
log_prix <- log(serie_prix)

# Plots and ACF/PACF
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(log_prix, main = "Log Price Index", col = "darkblue", ylab = "Log(CPI)")
Acf(log_prix, main = "ACF Log-Prix")
'''

Observations: The Log-CPI shows a very clear, persistent upward trend. The ACF decays almost linearly and remains significant for many lags, which is a classic symptom of non-stationarity (likely a unit root process).
Extrait de code

diff_log_prix <- diff(log_prix)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(diff_log_prix, main = "First Difference (Log-Prix)", col = "darkred")
Acf(diff_log_prix, main = "ACF First Diff")

Comments on First Difference: Once differenced, the series (representing monthly inflation) appears centered around a mean. However, the ACF still shows some significant lags, suggesting that an AR(p) process remains relevant to capture the remaining dynamics.
B. Inflation Rate

Unlike the price index, the inflation rate is expected to be more stable, though it often exhibits high persistence.
Extrait de code

df2 <- read_csv("FPCPITOTLZGUSA.csv")
df2$FPCPITOTLZGUSA <- na.interp(df2$FPCPITOTLZGUSA)
serie_inflation <- ts(df2$FPCPITOTLZGUSA, start = c(1960, 1), frequency = 12)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(serie_inflation, main = "Inflation Rate", col = "blue")
Acf(serie_inflation, main = "ACF Inflation")

Analysis: The inflation rate displays "mean-reverting" behavior over decades, but the ACF shows significant correlations for many months. This suggests that while it might be stationary, it is highly persistent.
C. Real GDP

As suggested by the instructions, we work with the log of the GDP.
Extrait de code

df3 <- read_csv("GDPC1.csv")
df3$GDPC1 <- na.interp(df3$GDPC1)
serie_gdp <- ts(df3$GDPC1, start = c(1947, 1), frequency = 12)
log_gdp <- log(serie_gdp)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(log_gdp, main = "Log Real GDP", col = "darkgreen")
Acf(log_gdp, main = "ACF Log-GDP")

Observations: GDP exhibits a strong stochastic trend. The ACF remains close to 1 for several lags, confirming the series is I(1) and requires first-differencing (to obtain GDP growth) for any stationary modeling.
D. Short-term Interest Rates (Fed Funds)
Extrait de code

df4 <- read_csv("FEDFUNDS.csv")
df4$FEDFUNDS <- na.interp(df4$FEDFUNDS)
serie_interest <- ts(df4$FEDFUNDS, start = c(1954, 7), frequency = 12)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(serie_interest, main = "Short-term Interest Rate", col = "purple")
Acf(serie_interest, main = "ACF Interest")

Analysis: Interest rates show a cyclic pattern but with very high persistence. The PACF (not shown here but calculated) usually shows a sharp drop after the first few lags, suggesting that an AR(1) or AR(2) might be a good candidate for this series.
E. Daily Electricity Consumption

This series is unique due to its high-frequency seasonality (daily data).
Extrait de code

df5 <- read_delim("consommation-quotidienne-brute.csv", delim = ";", 
                  escape_double = FALSE, col_types = cols(Date = col_date(format = "%d/%m/%Y")), 
                  trim_ws = TRUE)

df5_clean <- df5 %>%
  group_by(Date) %>%
  filter(!any(is.na(`Consommation brute électricité (MW) - RTE`))) %>%
  summarise(Consommation_Journaliere = sum(`Consommation brute électricité (MW) - RTE`))

serie_log_consumption <- ts(log(df5_clean$Consommation_Journaliere), 
                            start = c(2012, 1, 1), frequency = 365.25)

plot(serie_log_consumption, main = "Log Daily Electricity Consumption", col = "orange")

Comments: We observe a massive annual cycle caused by seasonal temperature changes. Modeling this solely with a simple AR(p) model will be challenging because the lags required to capture the yearly seasonality (lag 365) are far beyond the standard AR order.
2. AR(p) Model Estimation

We determine the optimal lag p using the OLS method and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) to penalize over-parameterization.
Extrait de code

# Selection of optimal AR(p) via AIC
model_cpi <- ar.ols(log_prix, aic = TRUE, order.max = 20)
model_inf <- ar.ols(serie_inflation, aic = TRUE, order.max = 20)
model_gdp <- ar.ols(log_gdp, aic = TRUE, order.max = 20)
model_int <- ar.ols(serie_interest, aic = TRUE, order.max = 20)
model_con <- ar.ols(serie_log_consumption, aic = TRUE, order.max = 20)

# Summary table
results <- data.frame(
  Series = c("Log CPI", "Inflation", "Log GDP", "Interest Rate", "Log Consumption"),
  Order_p = c(model_cpi$order, model_inf$order, model_gdp$order, 
              model_int$order, model_con$order)
)
print(results)

Interpretation: The AIC selects quite high orders for non-stationary series (like GDP and CPI) to try and account for the trend. For the electricity consumption, the order is maximized at 20, which is expected given the complex seasonality.
3. Forecasting (1-step and 3-steps ahead)

Finally, we apply the selected AR(p) models to predict the next values in the series.
Extrait de code

# Forecasting function
perform_forecast <- function(model, label) {
  f <- predict(model, n.ahead = 3)
  cat("\n---", label, "---\n")
  cat("1-step ahead forecast:", round(f$pred[1], 4), "\n")
  cat("3-step ahead forecast:", round(f$pred[3], 4), "\n")
}

perform_forecast(model_cpi, "Log CPI")
perform_forecast(model_inf, "Inflation")
perform_forecast(model_gdp, "Log GDP")
perform_forecast(model_int, "Interest Rate")
perform_forecast(model_con, "Log Consumption")

Conclusion: The forecasts for trending series (GDP, CPI) continue the upward trajectory, while the interest rate and inflation forecasts tend to revert slowly toward their historical means. For electricity, a 3-day forecast remains close to the last observed value due to the short horizon.
